ops.old: Research consistently estimates that social determinants of health — factors like income, education, housing quality, food security, neighborhood safety, and transportation access — drive between 50 and 80 percent of health outcomes. Clinical care accounts for roughly 20 percent.
ops.new: An analysis of U.S. county data (Hood et al., American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 2016) estimated that socioeconomic factors — income, education, employment, family and social support, community safety — account for about 47 percent of modifiable health outcomes, health behaviors for 34 percent, and clinical care for only 16 percent.

ops.note: Unattributed range replaced with a specific peer-reviewed estimate.

ops.old: By targeting the top 1 percent of cost drivers with wraparound services including housing assistance, transportation, medication management, and care coordination, the Coalition demonstrated significant reductions in hospital utilization. The model has since been replicated in dozens of communities and influenced the design of complex care management programs in Medicare and Medicaid.
ops.new: Its wraparound services included housing assistance, transportation, medication management, and care coordination. When the approach was tested rigorously, however, the result was sobering: a randomized trial of the Coalition's care-transitions program (Finkelstein et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2020) found 180-day readmission rates of 62.3 percent among enrolled patients versus 61.7 percent under usual care — no significant difference. The model still shaped complex care management nationally, and the trial is a standing lesson that promising before-and-after results need controlled evaluation.
ops.claim: Camden Coalition 'demonstrated significant reductions in hospital utilization'
ops.sources: Finkelstein A, Zhou A, Taubman S, Doyle J. 'Health Care Hotspotting — A Randomized, Controlled Trial.' NEJM 2020;382:152-162: 800 patients; 180-day readmission 62.3% vs 61.7%, no significant effect
ops.note: The RCT found no effect; claim reversed to what the evidence shows.

ops.old: These teams address SDOH needs alongside clinical needs, with a shared data system that allows providers across settings to track patients' social circumstances alongside their medical records. Vermont's model has been associated with reduced emergency department utilization, slower cost growth, and improved quality scores — providing one of the most comprehensive demonstrations that SDOH integration can work at a statewide population level.
ops.new: These teams address social needs alongside clinical needs. A peer-reviewed analysis of six years of Vermont all-payer claims (Jones et al., Population Health Management, 2016) associated the Blueprint's community-oriented medical-home model with lower expenditures and utilization while maintaining quality — one of the longest-running statewide examples of linking community supports to primary care.

ops.note: Uncited data-system claim dropped; outcome claim tied to its peer-reviewed source.

ops.old: The model operated across over 30 bridge organizations that screened over 800,000 beneficiaries for five core social needs: housing instability, food insecurity, transportation difficulties, utility needs, and interpersonal safety. Participants were randomized to awareness (referral information only), assistance (community navigation), and alignment (coordinating community services). Results showed that community navigation significantly reduced inpatient admissions and emergency department visits for beneficiaries with at least one unmet social need, validating the clinical and financial case for integrating SDOH screening into Medicare care delivery.
ops.new: Twenty-eight bridge organizations screened more than 1 million Medicaid and Medicare beneficiaries for five core needs: housing instability, food insecurity, transportation problems, utility difficulties, and interpersonal violence. In the Assistance Track, navigation-eligible beneficiaries (at least one need plus two or more ED visits in the prior year) were randomized to referral information alone or referral plus an offer of navigation; the Alignment Track was not randomized. CMS's final evaluation found that navigation lowered total health care expenditures — with fewer inpatient admissions and readmissions among Medicaid beneficiaries and fewer ED visits and ambulatory-care-sensitive admissions among fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries — even though rates of need resolution were similar to the control group.
ops.claim: AHC: 'over 30' bridge orgs, '800,000' screened, three randomized arms, navigation reduced admissions and ED visits for anyone with an unmet need
ops.sources: CMS Innovation Center, AHC Model Final Evaluation Report, Executive Summary (2026, cms.gov/priorities/innovation/data-and-reports/2026/ahc-final-report-exec-sum): 28 bridge organizations; >1 million screened; Assistance Track randomized (navigation vs referral-only control), Alignment Track not randomized; navigation lowered total expenditures; Medicaid lower inpatient admissions/readmissions; FFS Medicare lower ACSC admissions and ED visits; need resolution similar to control
ops.note: Counts, design and results corrected to CMS's final evaluation.

ops.old: The model demonstrated that community navigation significantly reduced inpatient admissions and emergency department visits for beneficiaries with at least one unmet social need, validating the premise that addressing SDOH can reduce healthcare utilization and cost.
ops.new: CMS's final evaluation found that navigation lowered total health care expenditures and hospital-based use among navigation-eligible beneficiaries (fewer inpatient admissions for Medicaid enrollees, fewer ED visits for fee-for-service Medicare enrollees), supporting the premise that addressing social needs can reduce utilization and cost.
ops.claim: Quiz explanation: AHC navigation reduced admissions and ED visits for anyone with an unmet need
